implementation_notes: The GoF roles collapse into the standard iterator library: a container exposes begin()/end() returning pointer-like iterators over a half-open range, algorithms take the (first, last) pair, and range-for desugars to it - there is no createIterator() method because iterators are cheap values and the end iterator doubles as the terminator (no iterator knows its own end). Iterator categories (LegacyInputIterator ... LegacyRandomAccessIterator, later concepts) plus std::iterator_traits encode which operations an algorithm may use. A hand-written iterator class is still justified when the type must be polymorphic in a way the category cannot express, or when the traversal state matches no container (custom tree walk, filtered view, generator-free state machine).
pitfalls: Iterator invalidation rules differ per container and are silent: vector reallocation, map insert/erase and deque push_front invalidate iterators in different ways, and using a stale one is undefined behaviour that often appears to work in debug builds.

The half-open [begin, end) contract is easy to get wrong in hand-written iterators: end is one-past-the-end and must never be dereferenced, and pointers are valid iterators for contiguous ranges, which blurs the boundary between iterator and storage.

An iterator type often leaks into the interface: a virtual function cannot return different iterator types per override, so polymorphic containers either fix the iterator type (coupling the interface to one representation) or need type erasure.

variants.name: C++20 ranges and composable views
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 generalizes the iterator pair into a range: the ranges library defines views (lightweight, non-owning ranges) and range adaptors that compose with the pipe operator into lazily evaluated pipelines, so traversal algorithm and filtering/transformation become one declaration instead of a cursor class. Range algorithms are eager, while adaptors apply as the view is iterated. Choose this when the toolchain is C++20 and the traversal is a composition rather than a single cursor; keep the plain begin/end pair at the API boundary if C++17 callers must remain supported.
pitfalls: Views refer to their underlying range: returning a view that refers to a local or temporary container dangles exactly like a returned reference (dangling-range diagnostics catch some, not all, of these).

The pipe syntax hides that filter/transform runs per element at iteration time, so a view over a container that is mutated in between sees the new state, and a single-pass input view consumed by the first loop is silently empty afterwards.

Adaptors require progressively stronger range concepts (forward_range, const-iterable, common range); mixing them produces long constraint errors far from the misuse, and a view over a range of references can outlive ownership expectations.

variants.name: C++23 std::generator coroutine range
variants.implementation_notes: C++23's std::generator turns a coroutine into a view/input_range: the traversal is written as linear code in a coroutine body and every co_yield produces one element on demand, so recursion over trees and graphs (co_yield std::ranges::elements_of(child)) reads naturally and a compiler-generated state machine replaces the hand-written cursor. It models input_range only (single-pass) and needs coroutine support; use it when the toolchain is C++23 and the traversal is easier to express recursively than as an explicit iterator with saved state.
pitfalls: A std::generator is input-only and single-shot: iterating it a second time yields nothing, so callers needing replay must materialize; forgetting this turns a refactor into a silent empty loop.

Coroutine frames allocate and the generator owns its frame: letting a generator capture state that dies between resumptions (or detaching it from a scope that cleans up) is the coroutine analogue of the dangling-iterator bug.
MSVC/GCC/Clang expose std::generator at different library versions even within C++23, so library and language floors must both be checked.
